### Reflection 

What Is Your BUSYness Hiding? 

BUSYness isn’t the problem. It is the solution, a remarkably effective, socially approved way of avoiding the discomfort of not knowing. 

Discomfort of not knowing whether your clients value you or merely tolerate you; whether your strategy is a real strategy; whether your best people are truly committed; what your competitors understand about your market that you don’t. 

These are difficult to know and costly not to know. BUSYness fills the space where that discomfort would live. 

The conversations that would surface real answers are slow conversations, and a BUSY organization has no patience for slowness. It doesn’t have a shortage of information; it has a shortage of the stillness in which information becomes understanding.

title: 5.a Version 1.0, Version 2.0, and the Discipline
core_lesson:
#### 5.a Version 1.0, Version 2.0, and the Discipline 

When we work with organizations on long-term transformation, we ask them to label their current business as Version 1.0 and the business they’re trying to build as Version 2.0. 

The 1.0 business will consume forty-eight hours a day if you let it. Version 2.0 won’t happen, won’t go beyond a good idea, unless you create dedicated time for it and protect that time. 

As Dr. Otto Scharmer of MIT says in his book on Theory U, the first transformation for creating a new reality is Transforming Perception. It precedes transforming self and transforming action, and it cannot be skipped. 

This is also why ROAR begins with Reflect, not Run. Everything else in this model depends on whether this first movement is genuine. 

Theory U makes one more distinction worth holding: the difference between discussion, debate, and dialogue. In most meetings, people either perform alignment or advocate for positions. 

A BUSY organization has plenty of discussion and debate, but almost no dialogue. 

Mr. Pandya, the Managing Director of a mid-sized manufacturing company headquartered in Mumbai, India, 

54 

Kill BUSYness 

made a decision that his leadership team initially received with scepticism. He announced that two days every month would be dedicated entirely to learning and reflection, no client meetings, no operational reviews, no routine work. 

The first few sessions felt uncomfortable. Leaders who were accustomed to non-stop activities had to pause, look, and reflect on their company, the market, and their collective mindset. Since some of them had attended our workshops earlier, they trusted the process. We encouraged them to collect data and see the market with fresh eyes, question their positioning in the market, their business plans, challenges, and opportunities. Mr. Pandya was in all the sessions himself, curious, engaged, asking thoughtful questions, sharing real concerns, and encouraging the team toward open and honest communication. He built a dialogue culture where everyone spoke, and everyone was heard. 

What emerged was not visible in any operational meeting. The leadership team began to see, with real clarity, that the organization’s next stage would need a different kind of leadership than the one that had brought it this far. They would need capabilities the existing team didn’t fully have. They also realised they had been benchmarking themselves against the best in India, not the best in the world, while wanting to compete against the global players. They acknowledged that their understanding of their most important customers was shallower than they had assumed. 

55 

Reflection 

That insight led to one of the most consequential decisions the company made in years: a deliberate, structured effort to bring in high-calibre external leadership for certain key roles instead of pushing all the responsibilities to the current people and hoping that they would learn on the job. Certain capabilities were not there in the organization, and it wasn’t appropriate to expect current people to somehow be able to do things that required different experience and exposure. 


![](/book_assets/media_1790181617777.pdf-0082-03.png)


Most leaders try to build Version 2.0 using Version 1.0 thinking. 

56 

Kill BUSYness 

Research consistently finds that more than half of the average week goes to activities that produce motion without progress (Asana, 2024). Deep, original thinking, the kind that produces real competitive advantage, requires protected time. 

5.b The Gap Between You and What Your Clients Actually Think Your dashboards show a lot of data. They don’t show what your clients think about you, whether they see you as a partner or a vendor. 

Most organizations mistake transaction history for relationship depth. They know what a client buys and what they pay. They don’t know what that client’s business is trying to become, what keeps their leadership team awake at night, or what would make them leave them for the competition OR sometimes in-house options. Assumptions, held long enough without examination, become beliefs. Beliefs, over time, become the walls of a box you can no longer see beyond.

title: 5.f The Age of Your Assumptions
core_lesson:
#### 5.f The Age of Your Assumptions 

Every organization develops assumptions about its market, its customers, its competitors, and its own capabilities. Most of these were valid once. 

The question is whether they are still valid and whether alternative perspectives exist. An organization too busy to challenge its own assumptions ends up running a past version of itself in a market that has already moved on. The gap between those two places doesn’t stay fixed. It widens every year you don’t look. 

Hint: Ask the leadership team to spend a month studying the market, meeting key stakeholders, and surfacing contradictory data, information that challenges your current assumptions about yourself, your competition, your industry, and the future.

title: 5.g The Listening Practice
core_lesson:
#### 5.g The Listening Practice 

Four levels of listening 

Dr. Otto Scharmer’s work describes four levels, and most organizational conversations never get past the first. 

Downloading: You already know what they’re going to say, so you listen just long enough to confirm it. This is the default mode of habitual listening without much conscious effort: reconfirming what you already believe, often while mentally composing your reply. 

59 

Reflection 


![](/book_assets/media_1790181617777.pdf-0086-02.png)


Factual listening: You notice what’s actually different from what you expected. This requires setting your assumption aside long enough to register a fact that contradicts it. 

Empathic listening: You listen from inside the other person’s experience instead of your own. You stop evaluating what they’re saying and start sensing why it matters to them. 

Generative listening: You listen from a kind of stillness that lets something genuinely new emerge, something never fully articulated before the conversation began. This is rare, and it cannot be rushed.

title: 6.a How Follow-Up Cultures Accumulate
core_lesson:
#### 6.a How Follow-Up Cultures Accumulate 

Nobody designed a follow-up culture deliberately. It accumulated, one loose promise at a time, one missed deadline absorbed without consequence, layer on layer until chasing became the rhythm of the organization. 

In teams where accountability is genuinely owned, followup messages are rarely needed. In teams where it isn’t, chasing people and deadlines becomes the most played game in town.
reflection_question: How does this apply to your organization?

title: 6.b The Two Cultures, Side by Side
core_lesson:
#### 6.b The Two Cultures, Side by Side 

- Customers. 

In a BUSY culture, customers are a transaction. Nobody is immersed in the customers’ world. 

In a High-Performance culture, the customers’ long-term objectives are not just managed; they are genuinely understood. Their dreams and challenges are studied continuously. Leaders in a high-performance Organization, stop asking how to get more business and instead ask how to partner with the customers and serve them at the core. 

- Accountability. 

In a BUSY culture, accountability is enforced. Work advances only after checking. 

In a high-performance culture, accountability is owned. Commitments are explicit. 

64 

Kill BUSYness 

- Standards. 

In high-performance companies, standards are nonnegotiable. 

Once you lower the standard, you’ve decided who you’re becoming. 

- The Future. 

In a BUSY culture, the future arrives as disruption, and the organization scrambles to respond. The High-Performance organization sees disruption early and moves first, because it is always scanning the landscape and looking for the emerging future, rather than firefighting the present. 

- Why People Show Up. 

In a BUSY culture, people are doing a job. Delivering at a level way below the collective capability, because that’s the level the culture has calibrated to. Again, a transactional relationship. 

In a High-Performance Organization, people are part of something they genuinely value. 

The gap between a BUSY culture and a High-Performance one is measurable. The finding from Chapter 2 bears repeating here: 70% of a team’s engagement is tied to the quality of the immediate manager (Gallup, 2025). The global employee engagement average is just 20%. That kind of engagement level is the product of a BUSY organization, not in sync with an inspiring purpose. 

65 

Ownership

title: 6.c NFR: No Follow-Up Required
core_lesson:
#### 6.c NFR: No Follow-Up Required 

NFR – No Follow-Up Required is the standard that separates BUSY cultures from High-Performance ones. 

No Follow-Up Required means in your organization, a commitment made is a commitment honoured. Leaders and teams operate with such clarity, ownership, and integrity that no follow-ups are required. People will commit thoughtfully, but once committed, it will be done. In case of breakdowns, pro-active communication is the norm. 

The evidence from these organizations confirms that once the leader personally models the standard, something in the organization’s nervous system begins to change. 

Within months, the evidence from these organizations confirmed something nobody had predicted: a significant increase in teamwork and mutual respect. When accountability becomes the norm, trust follows. 

If organizations stop chasing and start being NFR, they free up eight to twelve hours per person per week. That is a full working day returned to strategic work, relationship building, deep thinking, the very things that a BUSY organization can never find time for. 

The NFR System works through five phases: 

66 

Kill BUSYness 


![](/book_assets/media_1790181617777.pdf-0093-02.png)


1. NFRL – No Follow-Up Required Leader. If no one needs to follow up with you, you’re certified as an NFRL. 

2. NFRT – NFR Team – Your team becomes proactive in communication, and no follow-up is required. 

3. NFRD – NFR Department – Your department becomes reliable. 

4. NFRC – NFR Company – The whole company becomes trustworthy.

title: 6.d Culture Can Change
core_lesson:
#### 6.d Culture Can Change 

On 4 February 2014, Satya Nadella became CEO of Microsoft. The culture he inherited was what he called “know-it-all”, siloed departments protecting turf, leaders exhausted by internal politics, teams falling behind on every major platform shift (mobile, cloud, social). The company that had dominated personal computing was becoming irrelevant in the new world. Nadella’s first major declaration as CEO shocked many. It wasn’t a product announcement, a restructuring plan, or a financial target. He declared, “Our ability to change our culture is the leading indicator of our future success.” Culture first. The strategy would follow. 

The cultural shift from “know-it-all” to “learn-it-all” had to come first. Only then did the commercial transformation become possible. 

The numbers tell the story: Microsoft’s market cap grew from $300 billion when Nadella took over to approximately $3 trillion by 2024, a tenfold increase. Revenue grew nearly 3x. The stock price grew roughly 10x. 

Those numbers, though, are the outcome, not the cause. The cause was a CEO who understood that cultural transformation is the prerequisite for commercial transformation, that no strategy survives a culture that cannot sustain it. Transform the culture. Everything else can be built on that foundation. 

68 

Kill BUSYness 

Building the NFR Culture: Practical Leadership Behaviours What follows are not abstract principles. Each one describes a concrete change in behaviour that, when practised consistently by the leader first, begins to shift the organization’s relationship with commitment. 

- Slow down the making of commitments and the accepting of commitments. 

Make it a conscious activity. Ensure complete understanding on both sides of what’s being committed to, why it’s important, how it fits the bigger picture, what the process is for delivering it, and the timelines, support and resources required. 

- Create mutually agreed updates or check-ins. 

- For large and complex tasks, create timely progress check-ins. 

All of these are on the foundation of Shared Purpose, Aligned Strategy, Respect in Relationships, Culture of Accountability, and Discipline of Proactive Communication.
